ClinVar submitters as a rater study

Source: vignettes/clinvar-raters.Rmd
clinvar-raters.Rmd

These two public-domain subsets use ClinVar state 2026-10-19. The HRF subset includes variants in MEFV, MVK, NLRP3 and TNFRSF1A with at least two distinct submitters after the exact five-class filter. The genome-wide sample draws 1000 variants with at least 3 distinct remaining submitters, using seed 20261024 from a numerically sorted list. Filtering precedes both counting and sampling. Each selected variant retains all qualifying submissions, including multiple SCVs from the same submitter.

The ordered scale is Benign < Likely benign < Uncertain significance < Likely pathogenic < Pathogenic. Other terms are excluded, with counts in the packaged provenance. Gene lists come unchanged from variant_summary; the submitter identifier is the original submitter text. data-raw/make_clinvar_subsets.R checks the anchored source hashes and reproduces the stored files. Their SHA256SUMS includes QUELLE.txt. This article reads only installed data and makes no model calls.

Agreement and ordinal components

Variant maps to item and submitter to prompt, with a single model and block, and replicate one. Krippendorff’s alpha uses all submissions without modal reduction: weights = "unweighted" gives nominal alpha and weights = "linear" selects the ordinal metric. The reported row is all conditions, whose unit is the variant. Only variants with at least two submissions contribute pairable ratings.

Complete agreement means the same one of the five classes for every submission. Conflict means at least two of the three groups B/LB, VUS and P/LP, following ANK-46. Both proportions use variants with at least two submissions as denominator. Conflict is therefore not the complement of complete agreement: a B/LB or P/LP difference fails exact agreement without crossing a conflict boundary.

alpha_values <- function(d) {
  runs <- as_rater_runs(d)
  nominal <- msa_agreement(runs, levels = classes, weights = "unweighted")
  ordinal <- msa_agreement(runs, levels = classes, weights = "linear")
  c(alpha_nominal = nominal$alpha$alpha[nominal$alpha$scope == "all conditions"],
    alpha_ordinal = ordinal$alpha$alpha[ordinal$alpha$scope == "all conditions"])
}
pairable_counts <- function(d) {
  sizes <- table(d$variation_id)
  c(variants = length(sizes), submissions = nrow(d), pairable_variants = sum(sizes >= 2L),
    pairable_submissions = sum(sizes[sizes >= 2L]))
}
groups <- setNames(c("B/LB", "B/LB", "VUS", "P/LP", "P/LP"), classes)
analyses <- lapply(names(datasets), function(name) {
  d <- datasets[[name]]
  ratings <- split(d$classification, d$variation_id)
  ratings <- ratings[lengths(ratings) >= 2L]
  agreement <- mean(vapply(ratings, function(x) length(unique(x)) == 1L, logical(1)))
  conflict <- mean(vapply(ratings, function(x) length(unique(groups[x])) >= 2L, logical(1)))
  diagnostics <- character()
  fit <- withCallingHandlers(msa_fit(as_rater_runs(d), type = "ordinal", levels = classes,
                                    interactions = FALSE, link = "probit"),
    warning = function(w) {
      diagnostics <<- c(diagnostics, conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }, message = function(m) {
      diagnostics <<- c(diagnostics, conditionMessage(m)); invokeRestart("muffleMessage")
    })
  grr <- msa_grr(fit)
  components <- setNames(fit$vc$variance, fit$vc$source)
  list(agreement = data.frame(subset = name, as.list(pairable_counts(d)), as.list(alpha_values(d)),
                              full_agreement = agreement, conflict = conflict),
       fit = data.frame(subset = name, item = components[["item"]], prompt = components[["prompt"]],
         grr_pct_study_var = grr$summary[["grr_pct_study_var"]], converged = fit$converged, singular = fit$singular),
       diagnostics = data.frame(subset = name, diagnostic = if (length(diagnostics)) paste(unique(diagnostics), collapse = " | ") else "none"))
})

The fits use the default probit link without interactions. item is variant variance; prompt is submitter variance. Percent GRR uses study variation. The residual variance is fixed by the link, not an empirical estimate of repeatability between submissions. Unbalanced participation, correlated submissions from the same laboratory and differences in the assessed evidence limit an interpretation as independent random raters. This is an agreement study, not a clinical validation of individual classifications.

Sensitivity to review status

The specified sensitivity keeps only statuses beginning literally with “criteria provided”. It does not match “no assertion criteria provided”. It also excludes the higher status “reviewed by expert panel” and excludes “flagged submission”. The following counts show which statuses are present and retained. The initial submitter thresholds are not applied again; variants with one remaining submission cannot contribute to alpha.

status_counts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(datasets), function(name) {
  counts <- as.data.frame(table(review_status = datasets[[name]]$review_status),
                          responseName = "submissions", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  data.frame(subset = name, counts, retained = startsWith(counts$review_status, "criteria provided"))
}))
sensitivity <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(datasets), function(name) {
  d <- datasets[[name]]
  d <- d[!is.na(d$review_status) & startsWith(d$review_status, "criteria provided"), , drop = FALSE]
  data.frame(subset = name, as.list(pairable_counts(d)), as.list(alpha_values(d)))
}))

Literature comparison

This comparison is not an acceptance criterion. All values below are read from whole, hash-verified copies of ANK-42 through ANK-46. Counts, percentages, alpha and reported bounds retain their units. The labelled quantity paths identify each population and denominator; they should not be pooled into one agreement rate.

Yang et al. (ANK-42) combine classes into three pathogenicity groups or two actionability groups. Their clinical-testing subset from the later submission period uses actionability, not exact five-class concordance. Their complete agreement and majority-consensus rates answer different questions from each other and from the stricter complete agreement computed here.

Amendola et al. (ANK-43) compare laboratory criteria and ACMG-AMP criteria, then reassess agreement after consensus discussion. Their alpha population differs from the population of the initial and post-discussion counts, and the publication does not explicitly identify the alpha metric as nominal or ordinal. Harrison et al. (ANK-44) distinguish exact agreement, differences within B/LB or P/LP, and conflicts across those groups. Their reassessment changes the evidence and cannot be treated as a replicate of this snapshot.

Lazareva et al. (ANK-46) study whether a variant was tagged with a conflict at least once over the period 2018-04 to 2024-04, across genes with disease associations. That cumulative proportion is not a cross-sectional conflict fraction among multiply submitted variants.

Van Gijn et al. (ANK-45) provide the HRF comparison through a staged expert consensus workflow. The first-round no-consensus percentage is a lower bound, and the validation percentage is a voting rule. The abstract reports 804 consensus variants out of 858, while the Results counts sum to 803 from the validated and provisional groups. ANK-45 records this discrepancy; the table preserves the reported abstract value. No INSAID classification for an individual variant is distributed or used here.

Agreement with other submitters is not a correctness label for a variant. The different populations, grouping rules and reassessment procedures explain why these literature results are contextual comparisons rather than target values for either frozen subset. See vignette("validation") for the statistical engine checks and the ordinal simulation findings.
